## In 60 seconds

A biopotential front end must amplify microvolt-to-millivolt differences while the whole body floats at a much larger
**common-mode** voltage picked up from the mains. A differential amplifier passes the difference and rejects the
common mode; the ratio of the two gains is the **common-mode rejection ratio** (CMRR). Resistor tolerance limits it:
$(1 + G)/(4t)$ for a difference stage, improved by the input-stage gain of an **instrumentation amplifier**. Electrode
impedances that differ convert common mode to difference at the rate $\Delta Z/Z_{cm}$, however good the amplifier.
A **driven right leg** shrinks the common mode itself by $1 + G$. Noise adds in quadrature: the source's thermal noise
$\sqrt{4kTR}$, the amplifier's voltage noise, and its current noise through the source. The **Wilson central terminal**
is a resistor average that electrode impedances bias. The **converter** needs enough bits for offsets plus detail, and
averaging gains half a bit per doubling of the sample rate.

## From the field

- **Common mode is the enemy you cannot see.** Mains interference and its cures have a long engineering literature,
  including Huhta and Webster's paper on 60-Hz interference in electrocardiography [@huhta1973] and Winter and
  Webster's on driven-right-leg circuit design [@winter1983].
- **The central terminal is not a true zero.** Measured with a true unipolar recorder, the Wilson central terminal
  varied unpredictably through the cardiac cycle, and depends on balanced contact of at least four electrodes
  [@gargiulo2015].
- **Front-end quality shows in the signals.** In a multicenter blinded comparison of 218 signal pairs from 51
  patients, reviewers rated a new signal-processing platform superior to conventional sources for 75.2% of
  signals [@alahmad2021]. That is a reader-preference study, not a measurement of noise.
- **Know the acquisition chain.** A review for electrophysiologists covers electrogram acquisition
  [@venkatachalam2011].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $v_+$, $v_-$ input voltages; $v_d$ differential and $v_{cm}$ common-mode voltage; $A_d$,
$A_{cm}$ their gains; $R_1$–$R_4$ difference-stage resistors; $G = R_2/R_1$; $t$ resistor tolerance; $R$, $R_G$
input-stage resistors; $G_1$ input-stage gain; $Z_1$, $Z_2$ electrode impedances; $\Delta Z$ their difference; $Z_{cm}$
common-mode input impedance; $i_d$ displacement current into the body; $Z_{RL}$ right-leg electrode impedance; $G_{RL}$
driven-right-leg loop gain; $k$ Boltzmann's constant; $T$ temperature; $R_s$ source resistance; $e_n$, $i_n$ amplifier
voltage and current noise densities; $B$ bandwidth; $\Phi_i$ limb potentials; $R_W$ Wilson resistors; $N$ converter
bits; $m$ samples averaged.

### Differential and common mode

Any pair of inputs splits into a difference and a mean; an amplifier treats them with different gains:

$$
v_d = v_+ - v_-, \quad v_{cm} = \frac{v_+ + v_-}{2}, \qquad v_{out} = A_d v_d + A_{cm} v_{cm}, \qquad \text{CMRR} = \left\lvert\frac{A_d}{A_{cm}}\right\rvert
$$ {#eq-m14-cmrr}

Expressed in decibels, CMRR is $20\log_{10}$ of that ratio. A common mode of $v_{cm}$ appears at the output as if it
were a difference of $v_{cm}/\text{CMRR}$.

### The difference amplifier

One op amp and four resistors subtract: $v_-$ enters through $R_1$ with feedback $R_2$, and $v_+$ through the divider
$R_3$, $R_4$. With an ideal op amp:

$$
v_{out} = v_+\frac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4}\left(1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1}\right) - v_-\frac{R_2}{R_1}, \qquad \text{CMRR}_{\text{worst}} \approx \frac{1 + G}{4t}
$$ {#eq-m14-diffamp}

Matched ratios ($R_4/R_3 = R_2/R_1 = G$) give $G\,v_d$ and no common-mode gain. Resistors within tolerance $t$ in the
worst pattern leave $A_{cm} \approx 4tG/(1 + G)$, so 1% resistors and $G$ = 10 give 48.8 dB, and 0.1% gives 68.8 dB.
Random resistors rarely hit the worst case: drawn uniformly within tolerance, their median is about 14 dB better (lab
part A).

### The instrumentation amplifier

Put two op amps in front, joined through $R_G$. The difference sees gain $G_1$ while the common mode passes at unity:

$$
G_1 = 1 + \frac{2R}{R_G}, \qquad \text{CMRR}_{\text{total}} = G_1 \times \text{CMRR}_{\text{difference stage}}
$$ {#eq-m14-inamp}

So gain in the first stage buys rejection: with $G_1$ = 101 the 68.8 dB stage becomes 108.9 dB (lab part B). The input
stage also presents a high input impedance, which matters next.

**Key takeaways**

- CMRR is set by matching; gain before the difference stage multiplies it.

### Electrode impedance mismatch

Each input has a common-mode input impedance $Z_{cm}$ to ground, and the electrodes in series with it form two
dividers. If the electrodes differ, the common mode reaches the two inputs unequally:

$$
v_{d,\text{error}} = v_{cm}\left(\frac{Z_{cm}}{Z_{cm} + Z_2} - \frac{Z_{cm}}{Z_{cm} + Z_1}\right) \approx v_{cm}\frac{Z_1 - Z_2}{Z_{cm}}, \qquad \text{CMRR}_{\text{imbalance}} = \left\lvert\frac{Z_{cm}}{\Delta Z}\right\rvert
$$ {#eq-m14-imbalance}

This conversion happens before the amplifier, so no amplifier CMRR removes it; the two add as $1/\text{CMRR}$ values,
and the weaker path wins. A high $Z_{cm}$ (small input capacitance) and matched electrodes are the cures; see also Huhta and
Webster [@huhta1973].

::: {.demo #m14-d1 badge="exact"}

```{=html}
<script type="module" src="../demos/m14-d1-cmrr.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: worst-case resistor mismatch in a gain-10 difference stage (@eq-m14-diffamp) after an input stage of gain
  $G_1$ (@eq-m14-inamp), and a resistive electrode mismatch into a real common-mode input
  impedance (@eq-m14-imbalance); conversions add in the worst case. Tested against `epml.frontend`.
- Parameters: all values are adjustable illustrative choices, not those of any product.
- What it ignores: op-amp CMRR, input capacitance mismatch and phase, frequency dependence, cable shields.
:::

### The driven right leg

The body picks up a displacement current $i_d$ from the mains through stray capacitance; it returns through the
right-leg electrode. A driven right leg senses the common mode, inverts and amplifies it by $G_{RL}$, and drives the
right leg with it:

$$
v_{cm} = i_d Z_{RL} - G_{RL}\,v_{cm} \;\Longrightarrow\; v_{cm} = \frac{i_d Z_{RL}}{1 + G_{RL}}
$$ {#eq-m14-drl}

With a loop gain of 100, the common mode, and with it every conversion path above, falls by about 40 dB (lab part C).
The loop must be stable and current-limited; see Winter and Webster on its design [@winter1983]. Patient safety for
the drive circuit belongs to m15.

**Key takeaways**

- Mismatched electrodes convert common mode before the amplifier; only a high $Z_{cm}$ or a smaller $v_{cm}$ helps.
- A driven right leg attacks the common mode at its source.

### Noise

Independent noise sources add in power. Referred to the input, with source resistance $R_s$:

$$
e_{\text{total}}^2 = 4kTR_s + e_n^2 + (i_n R_s)^2, \qquad v_{\text{rms}} = e_{\text{total}}\sqrt{B}, \qquad R_{s,\text{opt}} = \frac{e_n}{i_n}
$$ {#eq-m14-noise}

The first term is thermal noise, derived by Nyquist [@nyquist1928]: about 4.1 nV/√Hz for 1 kΩ at 37 °C, with $k$ exact in
the SI [@codata2018]. The noise factor, total power over the source's own, is smallest at $R_s = e_n/i_n$. Small
electrodes raise $R_s$ (m13), so they push the thermal and current-noise terms up: halving the radius doubles $R_s$ and
raises thermal noise by $\sqrt2$. The electrode–electrolyte interface adds its own frequency-dependent impedance and
noise, which this model leaves out.

::: {.demo #m14-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m14-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m14-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m14-d2-noise.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m14-noise with white noise densities and a resistive source at 37 °C; Boltzmann's constant from CODATA
  [@codata2018]. Tested against `epml.frontend`.
- Parameters: amplifier noise densities, source resistance and bandwidth are adjustable illustrative choices.
- What it ignores: 1/f noise, the interface's capacitive impedance and its noise, filter shapes and quantization.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Noise adds in quadrature; the largest term dominates.
- Match the amplifier to the electrode: the noise factor is lowest at $e_n/i_n$.

### The Wilson central terminal

The central terminal joins the three limb electrodes through equal resistors $R_W$. Each electrode adds its impedance
$Z_i$, so the node settles at a weighted mean:

$$
\Phi_{\text{WCT}} = \frac{\sum_i \Phi_i/(R_W + Z_i)}{\sum_i 1/(R_W + Z_i)}
$$ {#eq-m14-wct}

With equal impedances it is the plain mean of m12 ([eq-m12-augmented](m12-surface-ecg.qmd#eq-m12-augmented)). One poor
electrode pulls it off: with $R_W$ = 5 kΩ and one 50-kΩ electrode the error was 0.24 (relative units, for limb
potentials spanning 1.2), and it falls as $R_W$ grows or buffers isolate the electrodes (lab part E). Even an ideal terminal moves with the
heart's activity [@gargiulo2015].

### The converter

An $N$-bit converter of full scale $V_{FS}$ after gain $G$ resolves steps of $V_{FS}/(G\,2^N)$; its quantization noise
is the step over $\sqrt{12}$ (m04, [eq-m04-quantization](m04-recording-chain.qmd#eq-m04-quantization)). Averaging $m$
samples of white noise and decimating improves the signal-to-noise ratio by:

$$
q_{\text{in}} = \frac{V_{FS}}{G\,2^N}, \qquad N \ge \log_2\frac{\text{span}}{\text{step}}, \qquad \Delta\text{SNR} = 10\log_{10} m \text{ dB}
$$ {#eq-m14-oversampling}

That is half a bit per doubling. A DC-coupled input must span the electrodes' offset potentials as well as the signal,
which drives the bit count: spanning an illustrative 200 mV in 1-µV steps needs 18 bits.

**Key takeaways**

- The reference is part of the measurement; electrode impedances bias it.
- Bits must cover offsets and detail; oversampling trades rate for resolution.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Every electrogram passes through a front end. Mains interference, baseline wander and
noise shape what can be annotated, especially low-amplitude signals in scar (m22, m23). The Wilson central terminal
references every unipolar chest lead and is not fixed [@gargiulo2015]. Signal quality differs between recording
platforms [@alahmad2021]. The standards for ECG technology are reviewed in a scientific statement [@kligfield2007],
and an EP-oriented review covers electrogram acquisition [@venkatachalam2011].

**What the evidence is.** Engineering analyses [@huhta1973; @winter1983; @nyquist1928], a device study
[@gargiulo2015], a blinded reader study [@alahmad2021] and reviews [@kligfield2007; @venkatachalam2011].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **What were the electrode impedances, and were they matched?** (@eq-m14-imbalance)
- **What is the noise floor in microvolts over the stated bandwidth?** (@eq-m14-noise)
- **What reference did the unipolar signals use?** (@eq-m14-wct)
- **Was a filter or notch applied, and where?** (m04)

## How experts think

When a recording looks noisy, ask in this order:

1. **Is it common mode leaking through?** Check electrode impedances and their match (@eq-m14-imbalance).
2. **Is the amplifier's CMRR the limit?** Gain before the difference stage helps (@eq-m14-inamp).
3. **Can the common mode itself be reduced?** Driven right leg, cabling, grounding (@eq-m14-drl).
4. **Which noise term dominates?** Thermal, voltage or current noise (@eq-m14-noise).
5. **Is the reference stable?** (@eq-m14-wct)
6. **Is the converter the floor?** Bits, offsets and oversampling (@eq-m14-oversampling).

One sentence to keep: **matching and impedance decide what the amplifier ever gets to reject.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Modes (@eq-m14-cmrr) | $v_d = v_+ - v_-$; $v_{cm} = (v_+ + v_-)/2$; CMRR $= \lvert A_d/A_{cm}\rvert$ |
| Difference stage (@eq-m14-diffamp) | gain $R_2/R_1$; worst-case CMRR $(1 + G)/(4t)$ |
| Instrumentation amplifier (@eq-m14-inamp) | $G_1 = 1 + 2R/R_G$; CMRR $\times G_1$ |
| Electrode mismatch (@eq-m14-imbalance) | error $\approx v_{cm}\,\Delta Z/Z_{cm}$; CMRR $= \lvert Z_{cm}/\Delta Z\rvert$ |
| Driven right leg (@eq-m14-drl) | $v_{cm} = i_d Z_{RL}/(1 + G_{RL})$ |
| Noise (@eq-m14-noise) | $e^2 = 4kTR_s + e_n^2 + i_n^2R_s^2$; optimum $R_s = e_n/i_n$ |
| Wilson central terminal (@eq-m14-wct) | weighted mean, weights $1/(R_W + Z_i)$ |
| Converter (@eq-m14-oversampling) | step $V_{FS}/(G2^N)$; averaging $m$: $+10\log_{10}m$ dB |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Boltzmann's constant $1.380649\times10^{-23}$ J/K | @codata2018 |
| 218 signal pairs, 51 patients, 75.2% rated superior | @alahmad2021 |
| Resistor tolerances, impedances, noise densities, 50 Hz, 10 mV common mode, 200 mV span | illustrative |
| CMRR values, noise totals, WCT errors, bit counts | our own code |

## Practice questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In your answer, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Define CMRR and say why biopotential amplifiers need a high one.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The ratio of differential to common-mode gain (@eq-m14-cmrr); the body's common-mode voltage from the mains can be far
larger than the signal, so even a small common-mode gain swamps it.

</details>

**Q2. What limits the CMRR of a four-resistor difference amplifier?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Resistor matching: worst case $(1 + G)/(4t)$ for tolerance $t$ (@eq-m14-diffamp).

</details>

**Q3. Why does an instrumentation amplifier's input stage improve CMRR?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It amplifies the difference by $G_1$ but passes the common mode at unity, so the difference stage sees a ratio $G_1$
times better (@eq-m14-inamp).

</details>

**Q4. The amplifier's CMRR is 120 dB, yet mains interference is strong. What else could it be?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Electrode impedance mismatch converting common mode before the amplifier, at $\Delta Z/Z_{cm}$ (@eq-m14-imbalance);
also cable pickup or a poor right-leg connection.

</details>

**Q5. How does a driven right leg work?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It senses the common mode, inverts and amplifies it, and drives the body through the right-leg electrode, dividing the
common mode by $1 + G$ (@eq-m14-drl) [@winter1983].

</details>

**Q6. Write the input-referred noise of an amplifier with source resistance $R_s$.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\sqrt{4kTR_s + e_n^2 + i_n^2R_s^2}$ per root hertz, times $\sqrt{B}$ for the rms (@eq-m14-noise) [@nyquist1928].

</details>

**Q7. At what source resistance is the noise factor lowest?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$e_n/i_n$: differentiate the noise factor with respect to $R_s$ (@eq-m14-noise).

</details>

**Q8. How does electrode size affect noise?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Smaller electrodes have higher spreading resistance (m13), raising thermal noise as $\sqrt{R_s}$ and current noise as
$R_s$ (@eq-m14-noise).

</details>

**Q9. Why is the Wilson central terminal not an exact average of the limb potentials?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Electrode impedances add to the averaging resistors, weighting the mean (@eq-m14-wct); and even an ideal average moves
with the heart's activity [@gargiulo2015].

</details>

**Q10. How many bits does a DC-coupled front end need?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Enough to span offsets plus signal at the needed step: $\log_2(\text{span}/\text{step})$ (@eq-m14-oversampling).

</details>

**Q11. What does oversampling by 16 buy, and under what assumption?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

12 dB, two bits, if the noise is white and uncorrelated between samples (@eq-m14-oversampling).

</details>

**Q12. Reviewers preferred one recording system's signals. What would you measure to confirm it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Input-referred noise over a stated band, CMRR with realistic electrode mismatch, filter responses and the reference;
a preference rating is not a measurement [@alahmad2021].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. $v_+$ = 1.002 V and $v_-$ = 0.998 V. Differential and common-mode voltages?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

4 mV and 1 V (@eq-m14-cmrr).

</details>

**S2. CMRR is 100 dB and the common mode is 1 V. Equivalent input error?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

10 µV (@eq-m14-cmrr).

</details>

**S3. Gain-10 difference stage, 1% resistors. Worst-case CMRR?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$11/0.04 = 275$, about 49 dB (@eq-m14-diffamp).

</details>

**S4. $\Delta Z$ = 10 kΩ and $Z_{cm}$ = 100 MΩ. Equivalent CMRR?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$10^4$, 80 dB (@eq-m14-imbalance).

</details>

**S5. A driven right leg with loop gain 99. Common mode reduced by?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

A factor of 100, 40 dB (@eq-m14-drl).

</details>

**S6. Averaging 4 samples of white noise. SNR gain?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 6 dB, one bit (@eq-m14-oversampling).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Interference paths.** Huhta and Webster's paper on 60-Hz interference in electrocardiography [@huhta1973].
  This module: electrode impedance mismatch.
- **The driven right leg.** Winter and Webster's paper on driven-right-leg circuit design [@winter1983]. This module: the
  driven right leg.
- **The central terminal over a beat.** Gargiulo's recordings of the Wilson central terminal with a true unipolar
  device [@gargiulo2015]. This module: the Wilson central terminal.
